The study uses a circular cylinder at Reynolds number 100 to model bluff body flow control.
Five pairs of WSLB actuators are arranged azimuthally at ±80°, ±40°, and 0° around the cylinder.
Each actuator pair consists of a suction slot on the windward side and a blowing slot on the leeward side, with zero-net-mass-flux actuation.
An array of 33 velocity sensors is placed 2 diameters downstream to measure wake velocities.
The DRL agent is trained using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm.
The cost function includes velocity deficit and actuator energy consumption with a weighting coefficient of 10^-4.
The DRL training converges after about 1000 episodes for the stationary cylinder.
The velocity deficit in the wake is reduced by 99.5%, leaving only a 0.29% discrepancy compared to uniform flow.
Hydrodynamic drag and lift forces are reduced close to zero under control.
The control strategy suppresses asymmetric vortex shedding and stabilizes the wake.
The same control strategy effectively reduces vortex-induced vibrations (VIV) in the cylinder.
VIV suppression reduces velocity deficit by 96.5% in locked-in and 95.9% in unlocked-in regimes.
Wake vortices are constrained near the cylinder and weakened downstream under control.
The lattice Boltzmann method is used for high-fidelity flow simulation accelerated by GPU.
Each simulation episode takes about 6 minutes on an NVIDIA Tesla K40c GPU.
Transfer learning from stationary to VIV cases reduces training time and improves control convergence.
Actuators at ±40° azimuth correspond to mean flow separation points, critical for effective control.
The study demonstrates active flow control can achieve hydrodynamic stealth by nearly eliminating wake signatures.
Hydrodynamic stealth reduces detectability by predators relying on flow sensing.
The control strategy balances hydrodynamic drag with actuator-generated thrust, achieving cruising status.
